#### `places_feature` {#places_feature}

<p class="fl-facts">required · feature identifier · edited on the connection, not in the form</p>

**The feature tried at every position in the search volume.**

A `namespace:id` that some file in the pack defines. Unresolved, the search fails before it visits a single position, and it says the same thing a search that ran out of positions says. Every attempt this feature makes is held back rather than written, so a delegate that succeeded at one position and was then thrown away when the search ran out leaves nothing behind at all.

#### `search_volume` {#search_volume}

<p class="fl-facts">required · group</p>

**The box of positions to try, relative to the origin.**

Both corners are offsets, so negative numbers are normal and are how you search below or behind the origin. Every position in the box is tried unless the search finishes early.

This field really does use `min`/`max` -- it is not a Range object, just a struct whose two members happen to be named that way.

#### `search_volume.min` {#search_volume-min}

<p class="fl-facts">required · groupList</p>

**The low corner of the search box, as [x, y, z] offsets.**

Not a minimum in the sense of a bound to satisfy -- it is one corner of the volume walked.

A 3-element [x, y, z] array.

#### `search_volume.max` {#search_volume-max}

<p class="fl-facts">required · groupList</p>

**The high corner of the search box, as [x, y, z] offsets.**

Not a maximum in the sense of a bound to satisfy -- it is the other corner of the volume walked.

A 3-element [x, y, z] array.

#### `search_axis` {#search_axis}

<p class="fl-facts">required · enum</p>

**The order positions inside the volume are tried in.**

It does not restrict the search to one axis: every position in the volume is still visited. What it picks is which axis is the outermost loop and which way each loop counts -- and because the scan stops at the first position that satisfies the wrapped feature (or at the required_successes-th one), that is what decides WHICH of several workable positions gets used. Two patterns are worth knowing because neither is guessable from the value names: the middle loop always counts upward (y for the x and z values, z for the y values), and the innermost loop takes its direction from the value rather than from its own axis. Each value below is just its own (outer, middle, inner) assignment.

Values, in the order the engine lists them:

- `-x` — Scans x descending on the outside, y ascending in the middle and z descending innermost.
- `+x` — Scans x ascending on the outside, y ascending in the middle and z ascending innermost.
- `-y` — Scans y descending on the outside, z ascending in the middle and x descending innermost.
- `+y` — Scans y ascending on the outside, z ascending in the middle and x ascending innermost.
- `-z` — Scans z descending on the outside, y ascending in the middle and x ascending innermost.
- `+z` — Scans z ascending on the outside, y ascending in the middle and x descending innermost.

#### `required_successes` {#required_successes}

<p class="fl-facts">optional · integer · absent: 1</p>

**How many positions have to work before the search commits.**

Everything the wrapped feature writes is held back until the target is reached; a search that runs out of positions first throws all of it away, so a partly-finished result is never left in the world.

0 loads and warns: the engine compares the success counter for EQUALITY after incrementing, so a counter tested only at 1 or more never matches 0 and the search exhausts. Whether the engine's own test is == or >= has NOT been established.
